This is a good question with regard to the use of social media, specifically microblogging. 

I don't know much about Instagram and people posting pictures of their stupid faces, but with regard to microblogging platforms like Twitter and Threads, we have Blue Sky. 

None of them, firstly, are indigenously locked platforms, or I would say nationally locked platforms. Twitter has given options to block geo-location-based posts from India, say, or Timbuktu, if you must, but that still invalidates it to the point that anybody can participate. 

Given that we have developed and deployed an indigenous microblogging platform, which is citizenu dot me, we have built-in features and functions:
- Verification by Aadhaar
- The ability to post with sentiment expression indicated as positive, neutral, or negative towards any topic
- Topical tracking of hashtags for statistical analysis
- The easy ability to search topics and trends, which Twitter used to have but has broken that functionality somehow

And over and above that, we hope to have an organic timeline to ensure an equal opportunity for visibility to all. We are not complicating or compounding our algorithm based on noise. 

Getting to the point of it, when it comes to blocking orders, we don't have a system in place for that at the moment. Naturally, being an indigenously deployed platform, we would have to concede to any orders, but there is a proposition that we could develop as we build our ecosystem. 

We would like to develop a system whereby, if a blocking order is given on a tweet, we'll enable the public to vote a majority yes or no if that is genuinely an offensive post. 

Again, there could be a window of opportunity for this balloting process. It could be an hour, it could be 45 minutes. These are all, systems that we would have to build around this new problem of incoming blocking orders.

Ideally, on an organically engaged platform, people will find that they are able to block one-to-one other individuals who they don't want to see or hear from. Those kinds of live metrics will also enable the government to decide whether a specific tweet needs to actually be blocked. 

What if there is an individual who's already blocked by a majority of other individuals on the platform? Is it necessary to block their post? Well, maybe it could be incredibly offensive or sensitive material, in which case, conceded, right?

Again, we are all about creative solutions. Our first one has been verification at the gate. Furthermore, we've integrated sentiment expression into our posts. We have geotagging. We have an organic algorithm for our timeline. 

For all we've built It's not going to be difficult to implement a bulletin board or balloting system for tweets that are notified, so people can go ahead and indicate back to the concerned government whether it's really offensive to them or they can deal with it. 

Sorry for the long-running explanation, but I just felt the issue deserved a detailed answer.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

In Portland, Oregon, there’s a small coffee shop called Cozy Bean.

During the day, it’s what you’d expect—people stopping in for a hot drink, soft background music, the usual warmth of a neighborhood café.

But something unexpected happens after closing time.

Once the customers leave and the lights are turned off, the owner turns them back on—but not for more business. He opens the doors again, this time for a different kind of guest: street dogs.

Since 2018, Cozy Bean has quietly offered shelter to stray dogs in the area. There's no advertising, no big signs, no posts asking for attention. It’s just something the owner does—every single night.

Inside, he sets out old blankets, cushions, and bowls of clean water. The dogs come in from the cold, some limping, some soaked from the rain, and they find a place to rest. They aren’t locked in or forced to stay. They just know they’re welcome—and they settle in like they belong there.

Some of the dogs are regulars. Others come and go. But every night, they have somewhere safe to sleep. A break from the noise and danger of the street.
The owner doesn’t do interviews. He doesn’t expect anything in return. He just makes space for those that have none.

It’s a simple act—opening a door, turning on a light, offering a little comfort. But it shows a level of compassion that’s hard to find in today’s world.

This isn’t about saving the world. It’s about doing what you can, right where you are. And that, in its quiet way, is something extraordinary.

The call came during second period. Calm, but with an edge. "Can you come down to Room 12? One of the eighth graders is refusing to remove his cap." 

When I got to my office, there he was. Jaden. Usually soft-spoken, respectful. But today he sat curled in the chair like he wanted to vanish. Cap pulled low. He muttered so quietly I almost missed it: "They laughed at me."

He told me kids in the cafeteria had made fun of his botched haircut. He slowly lifted his cap. His hair was butchered, lines jagged, and bald patches.

I stood and walked over to my cabinet and pulled out my old barber kit. Before I became a principal, I cut hair to pay for college. "Let me help, yeah?" I asked.

He nodded. I draped a towel over his shoulders and started shaping him up. 

As the first smooth line buzzed into place, he exhaled like someone finally let him breathe again. 

As I adjusted the angle for a final fade, I noticed something. Scars. Tiny, raised lines etched into the back of his scalp. I froze for half a second. "These... from something recent?" I asked softly.

He didn't answer right away. Then he whispered:
"That's where they hit me. Last year. When we were still at our old place." I turned the clippers off. "Who's 'they'?" I asked.

He didn't look at me. And then he said something that made my blood run cold "My mom's ex-boyfriend," he whispered, his voice so small it was almost swallowed by the quiet hum of the office. "He... he used to get mad. At her. At me. He'd throw things. The last time, it was a coffee mug." 

The clippers in my hand suddenly felt impossibly heavy. The botched haircut, the hat, the fear, it wasn't just about shame. It was about hiding. It was about survival.

"Jaden," I said, my voice steady despite the rage coiling in my gut. "Is he still around? Is your mom okay?"
He finally looked at me in the mirror, his eyes wide and haunted. "We left. A few months ago. We have a new apartment now. It's supposed to be better." 

He paused. "But he found us."
My blood ran cold. "When, Jaden?"
"Last night," he choked out, a single tear tracing a path through the tiny clipped hairs on his cheek. "He was waiting outside. He told my mom he was sorry.

He said he'd changed. She... she let him in." The haircut. It wasn't his cousin. It was him. A clumsy, cruel attempt at an apology, or worse, a mark of ownership.
I put the clippers down. The haircut was over. My real job was just beginning.

"Okay," I said, my voice leaving no room for argument. I put my hands on his shoulders, turning him to face me. "Here is what's going to happen. You are not going home on that bus today. You are going to stay right here with me. 

We're going to call your mom, and we're going to call some people who can help. People who make sure men like that go away and never come back. Do you understand?" He just nodded, a wave of relief so profound it seemed to uncurl his hunched shoulders.

For the next two hours, my office became a command center. I called Child Protective Services. I called the police. I spoke to Jaden's mother, who sobbed on the phone, admitting she was terrified but didn't know what to do.
When she arrived at the school, she wasn't alone. A police officer and a social worker were with her. They had a plan. An emergency protective order. A new place to go, a shelter with security, where he couldn't find them.
As Jaden got ready to leave with his mom, he stopped at my office door. His hair was perfect. But more than that, his eyes were clear. The fear was still there, but it wasn't hiding anymore.
"Thank you," he whispered.

"You're a good kid, Jaden," I said, my voice thick.
"You deserve to feel safe."

He reached up and touched the back of his head, where the scars were now hidden beneath the clean lines of his new haircut. "You know," he said, a small, hesitant smile on his face. "You're a pretty good barber."

This is a fictional story posted on Pinterest by Cecie Jay.

The clippers suddenly stopped.

I looked up.

Andre had pushed Theo’s hair aside and was staring at the skin behind his ear. He stayed like that for several seconds before lifting his eyes toward me in the mirror.

Something in his expression had changed.

I asked if everything was okay, but Andre only nodded and finished the haircut. The jokes stopped, though. Theo noticed it too and became strangely quiet.

When the cape came off, Theo ran toward the front window to look at the candy machine.

Andre leaned closer to me.

“Check behind his left ear when you get home.”

I frowned. “For what?”

Another customer was already walking toward his chair, and Andre lowered his voice. “Just look carefully. Don’t pull at anything until you know what it is.”

That was all he would say.

Ten minutes later, Theo was standing in our kitchen while I pushed his freshly cut hair away from his ear.

At first, I saw nothing except a small flesh-colored patch.

Then I touched it.

Something hard was underneath.

My stomach tightened.

I carefully lifted one corner and saw a tiny black disc, barely larger than a grain of rice, pressed against Theo’s skin.

“Theo, who put this here?”

His face changed instantly.

He looked down at the floor and said he didn’t know. When I asked again, more firmly this time, he rubbed his hands against his shorts.

“Maybe the man from school.”

I went cold.

“What man?”

Theo hesitated before answering.

“The one who said he knew Dad.”

My husband, Gavin, had passed away three years earlier.

I grabbed my phone and called the police.

The dispatcher told me not to remove the object and asked whether Theo and I were somewhere safe. I said we were home. She told me to lock the doors and wait.

text:
Two Muslim women journalists on Thursday alleged that they were beaten by Delhi police personnel in South Delhi’s Saket police station. The two journalists said that a police team detained them and took them to the Saket police station, where they were assaulted.The journalists were on assignment to cover an event attended by Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, following which the assault occurred, the journalists alleged. 

The journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafessa Khan alleged that they were dragged by their hair upstairs and were met with brutish assault for approximately 40 mins. 

“They dragged us upstairs by our hair and brutally assaulted us there. When they became exhausted from beating us, they stopped to take a break.”  Journalist Shaheen Khan told FoEJ Media. 

Both the journalists further claimed that on learning about their Muslim identity, the assault was intensified. 

“When they found out that we were Muslims, she said, ‘You’re Muslim? Now I’ll beat you even more'” Shaheen said. 

“She told me, ‘You’re Muslim? I’ll hit you three or four more times.’ She then struck me so hard with a lathi that the injury is still swollen.”  Nafeesa added, showing her bruises to FoEJ Media. 

Revealing the start of the assault, Shaheen said, “I was standing downstairs, speaking to my family over the phone and informing them about what had happened. Meanwhile, a female police officer approached me and demanded that I hand over my phone. When I told her, ‘Please tell me what happened; whatever you need to discuss, we can discuss it here,’ she replied, ‘I have a different way of talking. We’ll talk upstairs.’” 

“Listen to the language she used. She said, ‘I have a different way of talking. I’ll speak to you upstairs.'” Shaheen highlighted.

“She snatched my phone and started slapping me,” she added. 

Both the journalists further alleged that they were refused to have water even when they were falling to grasp the air due to the continuous assault. 

“When we asked, ‘Ma’am, please give us some water,’ she replied, ‘We will beat you thirsty,'” Shaheen alleged.

“Nafeesa’s condition deteriorated, and she collapsed unconscious. I told them that she needed medical attention, but no one paid any heed,” she added. 

The incident occurred on Thursday morning when the Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta attended the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket. 

The journalist said that they had gone to cover the event; however, they were stopped by police and taken to Saket police station, where the assault was launched. 

In an official statement, DCP (South) Anant Mittal described the allegations as “factually incorrect and misleading.”

“Claims suggesting otherwise, including allegations of assault for asking questions to the Hon’ble Chief Minister, are totally false, misleading, and baseless. Citizens and social media users are advised to refrain from circulating unverified and misleading information,” read the statement.  

The police said that despite multiple requests and instructions to remove the vehicles and clear the route, they refused to remove them. Following the security and safety protocol of the VVIP route, both the journalists were taken to the local police station for the inquiry, the police said, and the Hindustan Times highlighted. 

“In recent days, 4pm has been consistently raising serious questions and publishing reports on matters related to the Delhi government and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta. In such a context, it is natural to wonder whether today’s action is connected to those reports and questions in any way.” said Sanjay Sharma, the editor-in-chief of 4pm News Network. 

“Since when has asking questions of the Chief Minister become a crime? Since when has a journalist’s question become so dangerous for those in power? And can a journalist having ‘Khan’ in their name become a reason for assaulting them?” he posted on X. 

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

The incident was also condemned by the political leaders. Congress posted the video on X, while members of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) have condemned the alleged use of force against journalists and accused the government of failing to protect press freedom. Indian Youth Congress leader Darshan Kaushik speaking to FoEJ Media said, “It is extremely shameful that two girls were subjected to brutality after being asked about their religion. Even today, if they have to prove their loyalty to the country and the public, it is highly shameful.”

The Angulana resident was initially arrested by the Indian Navy while allegedly transporting 337 kilograms of heroin to India by sea. Police said he was imprisoned in Kochi, India, but escaped and returned to Sri Lanka by sea.

After returning, he was arrested in Wennappuwa and produced before the Marawila Magistrate’s Court. He was remanded and later released on bail. Police said he subsequently escaped from the custody of prison officers while appearing in court in connection with the case.

Officers of the Mount Lavinia Divisional Crime Investigation Bureau arrested him in Wadduwa in the early hours of September 30.

text:
A refused Soviet visa sent Mary’s BSA around the world

In October 1967, 26-year-old court reporter Mary Sievier left Selsey, West Sussex, on a 175cc Birmingham-built BSA Bantam. Nine years and more than 50,000 miles later, she had become the first British woman to circle the world alone by motorcycle.

The journey began during the Cold War with a rejection. Mary wanted to ride across the Soviet Union, but its authorities refused her a visa; she later recalled being told that seeing 15,000 miles of the country by bike was too much for a woman.

Her answer was to aim for India instead.

Mary had only learnt to ride that year. Two police motorcycle mechanics recommended the little Bantam because it was simple and light enough to put in a van if it failed. She spent four months learning to maintain it, packed budget panniers and left with £80.

She crossed Europe, survived a fall in Turkey and reached Kabul, Afghanistan. When the money ran low, her shorthand skills became part of the machine: she found office work, stayed for two years and saved enough to continue to India.

India did not become the finish. Mary shipped the BSA to Mombasa and rode through eastern and southern Africa. When she ran out of petrol in apartheid-era South Africa, several white motorists passed; a black father and son stopped and siphoned fuel from their own car.

Australia nearly ended it. The Bantam broke down on a remote stretch between Perth and Darwin while Mary had no water. A passing Land Rover brought help. The humble engineering choice kept paying back: despite thousands of rough miles, she later remembered suffering only two punctures on the entire journey.

After Australia, New Zealand and Southeast Asia, Mary reached Hong Kong and was ready to stop. David Smith, whom she would marry, persuaded her to complete the circle so she could say she had truly ridden around the world.

In 1976 she shipped the Bantam to Los Angeles, crossed the United States and sent it home from the east coast. There was no grand British reception. The bike went into her mother’s garage in Selsey, where salt air and time took their toll; it eventually spent years in boxes.

Mary finally told the full story in 2021. The Bantam was restored, she rode it again, and today it survives at the National Motor Museum in Beaulieu, Hampshire.

The Soviet ride deemed too much for a woman had become a solo lap of the planet—and the battered little BSA had waited in a shed for Britain to notice.

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. 🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo
